title: Small Tweaks for Making Chris Hulleman's Build Connections Intervention Work Even Better
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares adjustments that make Chris Hulleman's Build Connections intervention easier for students in its early rounds. Rather than hand out the polished worksheet, he displays simple warm-up instructions and talks students through what to list in Column A (things they value, their goals, and the kind of person they want to be) before moving to Column B (course content and skills). He emphasizes coaching the brainstorm aloud and setting a minimum of five items with a stretch goal of ten. He has found it difficult to connect world history content to values, but easy to connect the skills the course practices, such as studying and pop-up debating, to the person students want to be. His principle is that the first round should let students experience success, giving the teacher something to build on.
points: Talking students through each column of the brainstorm, instead of letting them work alone from a worksheet, makes the first round far more successful.
The most useful category in Column A is descriptors of the person the student wants to be, so spend extra time there.
Connecting course skills (not content) to students' values is easier and more convincing, particularly for a subject like world history.
Setting a minimum and a stretch goal for list length gives struggling students an achievable target.
quotes: But rolling the intervention out this year, both with my students and with some of the adult participants in my workshops these past months, I’ve found a few slight adjustments that make the early rounds of Build Connections much easier for my students.
Now, very importantly, I don’t just have students create these lists on their own. I have them put their pens in their hands, and then I talk them through different things they can write down.
I go on like this for a bit. And it’s this last category — descriptors of the person I’d like to be — that I find very, very helpful with the rest of this activity. So go big on that part.
I give 1-2 minutes for students to tap themselves out for Column A. I emphasize that a minimum goal is 5 (or if a lot of them are struggling, I’ll say 4 or 3) and that a stretch goal is 10.

The benefit of the tweaks I’m using this year — coaching participants through broad-level values and broad-level course skills — is that more participants succeed in the first round of build connections than I’ve seen succeed in the past. I’ve found that it’s pretty hard to connect world history content with one’s values — not impossible, but hard — but it’s pretty easy to connect the skills my course has students practice (studying, keeping track of assignments, doing homework, asking questions, pop-up debating) to the kinds of people they want to be.

Just like with the first pop-up debate, I think the goal of the first build connections exercise is for students to experience some success. From this humble foundation, an attentive teacher can build all kinds of beautiful things.
